notes: “A double portion” is a customary understanding of the difficult Hebrew expression “one portion, appayim.” Its exact force is uncertain.
The Hebrew places Hannah’s rising after the eating and drinking at Shiloh. It need not mean that she herself ate, after verse 7 says she would not.
The pinned Hebrew says “his word,” without specifying a previously quoted divine promise.
The Hebrew has “three bulls,” followed by “the bull” in verse 25. A different textual reading gives “a three-year-old bull.” The draft retains the pinned Hebrew.
The final Hebrew verb is singular, “he worshiped.” The man or boy meant is not expressly named.
vocabulary: LORD of Armies — YHWH tseva’ot
A divine title also traditionally rendered “LORD of Hosts.”
Ask and give over — sha’al
Related forms connect Hannah’s request, Samuel’s naming, and his lifelong dedication. The naming explanation is wordplay, not a full etymology.
Ephah
An ancient dry measure, used here for flour.

notes: “By him” follows the traditional reading. The written form has “not,” producing a different and difficult clause about the weighing of deeds.
The Hebrew repeats the asking/giving-over language of chapter 1. The wording and the subject of the final verb are difficult.
Verse 24 may instead accuse the sons of causing the LORD’s people to transgress. “God can intervene” in verse 25 may also refer to divine judgment or a judge’s mediation.

“Arm” represents strength and family power. Verse 32 can also be understood as seeing a rival in the dwelling. Verse 33 literally says the household’s increase will “die as men”; “in the prime of life” is a contextual reading.
vocabulary: Horn — qeren
An image of strength and raised standing. Hannah’s own horn and the anointed king’s horn frame the prayer.
Sheol
The realm of the dead; the poem pairs descent with being raised up.
Ephod
A garment associated with sacred service; here it is made of linen.
Anointed — mashiaḥ
Someone marked out by anointing. The passage does not name the future figure.

sections.1: Samuel learns whose voice he hears

notes: The pinned Hebrew reads “bringing a curse on themselves.” Another textual understanding is “blaspheming God.” The wording is not silently changed here.
To let words “fall to the ground” is to let them fail or go unfulfilled.
vocabulary: Word — davar
Can mean a word, message, or matter. Hearing and carrying the LORD’s word shape Samuel’s calling.

notes: The Philistines’ speech moves from a singular expression for deity to explicitly plural “gods.” Their recollection of Egypt and the wilderness is retained as their speech.
Ichabod evokes the absence of glory. “Gone into exile” carries the force of the verb galah and is repeated in the woman’s final words.
vocabulary: Cherubim
Sacred throne-associated figures; the title links the ark with the LORD’s enthronement.
Be men
The source uses a gendered military call to courage, retained within the Philistines’ speech.

notes: “Only his trunk remained” gives the sense of the difficult phrase “only Dagon remained.”
The written and traditional reading forms use different terms for the swellings or tumors. Neither identifies a modern disease with certainty.
Ekron’s people speak in the singular, “me and my people,” as a communal voice.
vocabulary: Heavy hand
An image of overpowering pressure. Heavy/light and honor language recur in 6:5–6.

sections.19: Who can stand before the LORD?

notes: The pinned Hebrew has “great Abel,” a difficult expression. “Great stone” follows the object described in verses 14–15; this is a contextual textual correction.

The Hebrew gives the numbers in the unusual order “seventy men, fifty thousand men.” They are retained as a combined total, fifty thousand and seventy, rather than silently omitting fifty thousand. The number and its transmission require further textual review. “Looked into” may also be “looked at.”
vocabulary: Reparation offering — asham
An offering acknowledging guilt and making amends. Here the Philistine advisers prescribe gold objects.
Heavy hearts
The Hebrew uses the same root as “heavy hand” and “honor” nearby. Here it means stubborn refusal to respond.

notes: The difficult verb describes lamenting or yearning after the LORD. The twenty years mark the time leading into this account, not necessarily the ark’s entire stay.
The passage describes pouring out water but does not explain the ritual’s meaning.
“Thus far” can point to help up to this time or to this place.
vocabulary: Ebenezer — even ha‘ezer
“Stone of help.” Samuel’s explanation makes the name a memorial of help received.

notes: “How the king will treat them” renders mishpat, which can mean judgment, right, or established practice. Here it introduces a warning, not an endorsement of each royal action.
The pinned Hebrew says “your best young men.” A different reading has “your best cattle.”
vocabulary: Take — laqaḥ
The repeated verb accumulates: sons, daughters, land, produce, labor, and finally the people themselves.

notes: The Hebrew may mean “everything desirable in Israel” belonging to Saul, or “all Israel’s desire” directed toward him and his family.
The description of what accompanies the leg, and the wording about its reservation, are difficult. Samuel is understood to resume speaking after the cook sets it down.
vocabulary: Shekel
A measure of silver by weight, not a minted coin here.
Seer and prophet
The narrator explains the older and newer terms; the translation retains both.
High place — bamah
An elevated worship site. Its mention here is not itself a narrator’s judgment on the sacrifice.

notes: Gibeath-elohim means “hill of God.” The expression rendered “garrisons” can refer to Philistine posts or officials.
“Who is their father?” is left as a question. It may challenge the assumption that prophetic activity depends on family background.
The provisions of kingship are recorded but not quoted here. They should not simply be equated with every action warned of in chapter 8.
vocabulary: Anoint — mashaḥ
Pour or apply oil to mark someone for an office; compare David’s anointing in 16:13.
Inheritance — naḥalah
Here the LORD’s own people are described as his inheritance.

notes: Nahash’s demand names physical mutilation and the disgrace he intends to impose on all Israel.
The dismembered cattle and threat belong to Saul’s summons. The narrative also attributes the people’s terror to the LORD.
vocabulary: Covenant — berit
Here a binding agreement of political submission, as the offer to serve Nahash makes clear.

notes: Bedan is the name in the pinned Hebrew. The list is not silently changed to match a familiar list of judges. Samuel also refers to himself by name.
The Hebrew’s conditional sentence is compressed. This rendering takes following the LORD as the outcome of the stated obedience; it does not add an unexpressed promise of prosperity.
Literally, “against you and against your ancestors.” “As it was” makes the comparison intelligible. The draft does not replace “ancestors” with “king.”
vocabulary: Righteous acts — tsidqot
Acts displaying what is right, here recounted as the LORD’s saving dealings with Israel.
Empty things — tohu
What is insubstantial or futile; the repeated word stresses their inability to help.

notes: The transmitted Hebrew literally gives Saul’s age as “one year” and says he reigned “two years.” The regnal formula appears damaged. Ellipses mark information that cannot be recovered securely; no age or complete reign length is supplied.
“Garrison” may mean a Philistine official or post. The report in verse 4 credits Saul with the attack Jonathan carried out.
Thirty thousand chariots is the pinned Hebrew number, retained despite its difficulty beside six thousand horsemen.
The identities of some hiding places are uncertain, especially the word rendered “cellars.”

The tool names and price wording are difficult. A pim is an ancient weight; the translation retains it rather than assigning a modern price. “Three-pronged forks” is one understanding of the phrase that includes “three” and “fork.”
vocabulary: After his own heart
Someone corresponding to the LORD’s purpose or desire. The expression does not by itself assert a faultless character.

notes: The area is described in terms of a furrow and a pair of oxen. Its exact size is uncertain; no modern acreage is imposed.
“Terror from God” can also function as an expression for an immense terror. The earth’s shaking is stated separately.
The pinned Hebrew says “ark of God.” This is retained even though an ephod appears in verse 3 and the priestly inquiry in verse 19 makes the wording difficult.
The short Hebrew request is literally “Give tamim,” meaning complete, sound, or true. The exact form of the inquiry is uncertain; the next verse explicitly describes casting between two people.
Jonathan’s “Here I am, to die” can also be heard as an incredulous question. The people redeem him; no payment or substitute is specified.
The final verb normally concerns declaring guilt or doing wrong. “Inflicted punishment” preserves that sense in this military summary; the exact force remains uncertain.
The compressed genealogy is understood to make Ner Saul’s uncle and Abner Saul’s cousin. The wording can also attach “Saul’s uncle” directly to Abner.
vocabulary: Tooth of rock
The Hebrew’s image for the sharp crags flanking the pass.
Redeem — padah
Here to secure Jonathan’s release from the threatened death.

sections.10: Saul and Samuel confront each other

notes: The command expressly includes women, children, nursing infants, and animals. “Devote to destruction” does not reduce those deaths to a metaphor.
The word rendered “fattened animals” is uncertain; it may denote a valued class of animals, sometimes understood as second-born animals.

The same Hebrew root, naḥam, underlies “regret” and “change his mind.” The chapter speaks both of the LORD’s regret over Saul and of the firmness of the announced rejection. Both statements remain in the text.
Agag’s manner of approach is uncertain: “confidently” or “delicately,” but also understood as “trembling.”
vocabulary: Devote to destruction — ḥaram
Place under a ban that, in this command, entails destruction and death.
Household gods — teraphim
Cult objects named here beside divination and wickedness.
Glory of Israel — netsaḥ Yisra’el
A divine title; the first word can suggest enduring eminence or strength.

sections.6: The LORD looks at the heart

notes: The Hebrew contrasts seeing “to the eyes” with seeing “to the heart.” The draft supplies the implied divine comparison without turning “heart” into outward attractiveness.
“We will not sit down” takes the verb in the setting of the sacrificial meal; “we will not turn aside” is also possible.
“Ruddy” describes a reddish appearance; the text does not specify red hair.
“Harmful spirit” renders ruaḥ ra‘ah. The narrative attributes it to the LORD and describes torment and relief; it does not provide a modern medical diagnosis.
The servant calls David a warrior here. This description is retained without harmonizing it with later portrayals of his youth or inexperience.
vocabulary: Spirit — ruaḥ
The Spirit rushes upon David as earlier upon Saul; the following verse describes departure from Saul.
Breathe freely — rawaḥ
The word for relief echoes the sound of ruaḥ, “spirit,” in the same sentence.
